fix.before:
Images of Mercury and of Minerva — he the god of Eloquence, she of Prudence, inventress of the good arts; signifying that Eloquence and Prudence must needs be joined together, if words are to be of benefit to human actions.

MINERVA

It is said that among the marvellous things given by God to human Nature, two are greatly to be admired: one is speech, the other the use of the hands. For the one, expressing the mind's conceptions with marvellous force, persuades others of what it wishes; the other, with much industry, puts into effect all that can preserve men's lives, and defend them, as are all the arts already discovered, or that will be discovered in the future. And because fine speech does not benefit, but rather harms, and does evil whenever it is not accompanied by good will and by prudence, nor can prudence be of use to the world when it does not know how to persuade others to flee evil and follow good, and to do those things that are needful to civil life, the ancients showed this by coupling together Mercury, of whom I have already spoken, and Minerva, of whom I shall now speak, held to be the Goddess of prudence, and inventress of all the arts. And therefore, joining together the statues of both these Gods, they made of them one, and called it by a Greek word Hermathena, because the Greeks call Mercury Hermes, and Minerva Athena, and they kept it in the Academies, to show to those who exercised there that eloquence and prudence must be joined together, since the one by itself profits little, and the other by itself likewise often harms, and perhaps always, as Marcus Tullius discourses at some length at the beginning of his work On Invention, who also writes to his Atticus of this statue, as I have said, in this manner: "Your Hermathena pleases me greatly, and is so well placed in the Academy that it seems to hold it entirely." Wishing, then, to make Minerva, either alone, or accompanied by Mercury, she should be made with an almost masculine face, and very severe in aspect, with eyes of sky-blue colour, which Homer always gives her as her own. And Pausanias, after having written of a certain image of Minerva that was in Athens in the temple of Vulcan, adds that he had

found a certain fable, which makes her the daughter of Neptune, and that she had sky-blue eyes, because such were also her Father's. But Cicero, where he speaks of the nature of the Gods, says that Minerva's eyes were grey-green (caesii), and Neptune's blue (caerulei), which might show some difference between them, but I do not believe, however, that it was great, for both words among the Latins signify a light greenish colour, such as is seen in the eyes of cats and owls; unless they wish perhaps to say that in Minerva's eyes there was a more fiery brilliance, similar to that shown by the eyes of Lions. Let her likewise be made armed, with a long spear in hand, and with a crystal shield on her arm, as Ovid does, who has her depict herself in this very way, when she competes in embroidery against Arachne, saying, continuing that design.

She makes herself with spear, and with shield, and arms
Her head with a helmet, and her breast with a breastplate,

Which things show the nature of the prudent man, as I shall say later. Claudian too, and others, have described Minerva in the same manner, perhaps taking, as they have often done with many other things, the likeness from Homer, who, when he has her, persuaded by Juno, go to aid the Greeks against Mars, who then fought for the Trojans, describes her in the form of a valiant warrior, and gives her a helmet on her head all gilded, because the wit of the shrewd man, armed with wise counsels, easily defends himself from whatever might harm him, and shines entirely in the fine and worthy works he does. And the gold upon Minerva's helmet also signifies that she is often taken for the divine splendour which illuminates human intellects, and from which comes all prudence, and all knowledge. It was also imagined that Minerva was born from the head of Jove, as Pausanias writes, stating there was an image of this on the acropolis of Athens; Vulcan having opened it for her with a sharp diamond axe, without the service of a wife, because the intellective power of the soul resides in the brain; and she descends, and all her knowledge, from the supreme intellect, which is Jove: since all wisdom comes from God, and is born from the mouth of the Most High, not from these low and earthly things shown through Juno. And this is a better disposition than that which Martianus made in contempt of women, who, perhaps not being too great a friend of theirs, says, imagining that Minerva was born without a mother, because women have no counsel, nor any prudence; or perhaps he said this so as to follow Aristotle, who writes in his Ethics that women have no good counsel at all. Whom I do not dare to oppose, but I say well that many women in our times show themselves so prudent,

As for her, to return to his design, Apuleius places upon her helm a garland of olive, for this tree was given as her own by the ancients, because she was its discoverer, as Virgil also calls her, and as the fable tells of the contest that was between her and Neptune over the possession of Athens; where Herodotus writes that it was that same olive which Minerva then made spring up, and which burned together with the City already burned by the Persians, but that on that same day it put forth new shoots again, and grew to the height of two cubits. And some say that this was so feigned because Minerva was the first to show the way of pressing oil from olives, and also because the sciences cannot be acquired without frequent study and long vigils. Whence it is read that also in Athens there was dedicated to this Goddess a golden lamp, which burned continually, yet they put in no more oil than once a year, and this was, says Pausanias, because the wick was of a certain kind of flax that is not consumed by fire. And the same author relates that among the Corinthians, when Epopeus, for a certain victory, had made a temple to Minerva, he prayed her to show some sign of holding it dear, and that straightway there before the dedicated temple there sprang forth from the earth a shoot of olive. Whence it may be seen that rightly was the olive given to her, not only for the study of knowledge alone, but also for the practice of the arts discovered by her, such as spinning, sewing, weaving, and doing other things proper to women. For which the Greeks had a great wooden statue of this Goddess seated upon a high seat, holding a distaff with both hands: and the Romans, on a certain day of the feasts celebrated in March to Minerva, had the mistresses feast their maidservants, and serve them with their own hand, as if wishing to show that they acknowledged the benefit they drew from their maidservants through spinning, weaving, sewing, and doing the other things of which she had been the inventress; and that the maidservants likewise should have from her this reward for the labors endured all year in the arts found by her. The Owl too was at times placed upon Minerva's helm, as a bird proper to her and so loved by her that, whether upon her head or at her feet, she almost always has it with her; the reason for which some hold to be that in Athens, a city dear to this Goddess above all others, as the name shows, which she had in common with it, for the study of the sciences and the good arts, which there had already long flourished, there was a great abundance of these birds. Whence arose the proverb of "carrying owls to Athens," said of those who wish to give another that of which he already has great abundance. But the fables say that Minerva first loved the Crow, having made her become a bird from a beautiful maiden, who was

had first been a beautiful maiden, to defend her from the force of Neptune, who, having fallen in love with her, chased after her along the seashore, and kept her in his service until she accused the daughters of Cercops: whereupon the Goddess, angered then at the sorry office performed by this maiden, straightway made her, who had before been white, turn black as she is now, and drove her away from herself, and took the Owl in her place, whence there arose, and still endures, a most grave enmity between these two birds. And the Owl signifies the wisdom and good counsel of the prudent man, as is read in Justin, that an Owl having flown onto the spear of Hiero the first time that, still a youth, he went to war, it was interpreted that he would be of very shrewd counsel; and it proved true, for he became King of Syracuse, although born of low station. And because Minerva's eyes are of the same color as the Owl's, which sees very well by night, it is understood that the wise man sees and knows things however difficult and hidden they may be, and that, having lifted from his mind the veil of lies, he penetrates to Truth with the sight of the intellect; for she remains hidden, and does not let herself be seen by everyone: whence Democritus placed her in the depth of a well, saying that from there she never came out, unless Time, or Saturn her father (as Plutarch says), drew her out of it at times. And Hippocrates, writing to a friend of his, depicts Truth in the form of a woman beautiful, tall, honestly adorned, and all bright and shining, but most of all in the eyes, for these seem two most lucid stars, and he adds then concerning Opinion, that she is likewise a woman, but not so beautiful, nor ugly either, but shows herself all bold and quick to seize upon whatever presents itself to her. In Epiphanius it is read that certain Heretics depicted Truth with Greek letters in this manner. They set it that alpha and omega were the head, and beta and psi the neck, and so, coming down, they formed the whole body, always placing those two letters that, in order, come closest to the first and to the last. And Philostratus, saying that Truth was painted in the sacred cave of Amphiaraus, makes her clothed in the whitest garments, and elsewhere then calls her the mother of Virtue. Who was likewise believed a Goddess by the ancients, and worshipped, and to her, as to the other Gods, the Romans set up a temple before that of Honor, which, having been vowed to both of these by Marcellus, as Valerius Maximus relates, had to be made into two, because the Pontiffs said that religion did not allow a single temple to be dedicated to two Divinities: since, should some prodigy occur in it, one could not know to which of the two the sacrifice ought to be made. So that to Virtue and to Honor was given each its own separate place, and into this latter none could enter save by passing through the former, wishing thereby to show that there is no other way to acquire honor than that of virtue, as that is the

for the prudent man ought not to waste time in many vain words; but, keeping silent, must consider things very well before reasoning about them, and then say of them only what is needful. This perhaps the statue of this Goddess that was among the Messenians meant to show, which, as Pausanias describes it, held a Crow in its hand, as though to say that speech ought to be so held in the hand of the wise man, that he may loosen or restrain it according to whatever occasion presents itself as the need requires. Minerva also had a long spear in her hand, as I said, which all the Poets give her; and Apuleius likewise describes her as brandishing this in her hand, and, raising her arm, lifting her shield, and makes two go with her, like children, who with bare knives in hand seem to go threatening: of whom one is Dread, the other Fear, for wars are never without these. Wherefore Statius, imagining that Mars, commanded by Jove, goes to stir up war between the Argives and the Thebans, says that he took Dread and Terror with him, and made them go before him, and describes him in part, and in part depicts the feelings that come from him, in this manner.

From the cruel rabble that surrounds him he chooses
Terror, and sends him before on horseback,
Whose power none can match,
In making others fear, let alone surpass him.
Through him it seems that man scorns the truth,
If in the timid breast there come to dwell
The horrendous monster, who has voices without number,
And hands ever ready and bold for evil.
Not one alone is always his face,
But many, and all in varied aspects,
Which change at every hour, provided it please him
To match them to his dreadful words;
Which drive so forcefully into human hearts
That they are compelled to give them full belief.
And with such dread he often assails

The Cities, which then believe every evil,
Will believe that there is no longer but a single Sun,
And what is not shall seem to them a vision,
If wretched mortals to the words
Of dread Terror, rarely true,
Lend their ears, and believe that a cloud
Steals away the stars, whereby we must all then fall,
That the earth trembles in fear, and quakes entirely;
And with it the forests too are shaken.

Pausanias states that Terror was made in two ways by the ancients: one with a Lion's head, which was so carved, as he says, among the Eleans on the shield of Agamemnon: the other with the face and dress of a woman, but more frightful than can be told. And such an image of Dread the Corinthians dedicated to the children of Medea, slain by them on account of the pernicious gifts which they bore to the daughter of Creon, whereby she perished together with the whole royal house. But Fear was not always believed to be harmful, for Plutarch writes that it was worshipped by the Lacedaemonians, not because they feared it, as they did certain other Demons, whom they wished kept far from the city, but because they thought that the Republic was preserved by it, when the laws and the Magistrates were held in fear. Whence it was that the Ephors, who were the highest magistracy, upon entering office, at once (as Aristotle says) commanded, and had it proclaimed throughout the city, that everyone should shave his beard and be obedient to the laws; so that they themselves should not be forced to do harm to any person, and they did this to accustom the young to obey even in trifling matters. Besides this, the ancients did not believe that true courage lay in fearing nothing at all, but rather in being afraid to do something unworthy: and they held that he ought to be bolder against enemies who feared to offend the laws, than he who took no account of them at all; and that the fear of acquiring a bad name made men stouter in bearing every toil and every danger. And this is the fear that peoples ought to have; and for this the Lacedaemonians placed the temple of Fear beside the house of the Ephors. And of this perhaps Tullus Hostilius too, King of the Romans, had understanding, when he ordained (as Lactantius relates) that Fear and Pallor should be worshipped together, since it rarely happens that he who is afraid does not turn pale. And well did he deserve, having found them so fine, as Lactantius himself says, to have his Gods always with him, and that they should never abandon him. But returning to Minerva, she shows, while brandishing the spear, and raising the shield with the company that Apuleius gives her, the threats of war; and if we consider it

we consider it in peace, the shield, which was of most lucid crystal, and covered the body from whatever might have come to offend it, showed that the mind of the prudent man is covered by earthly limbs only so as to guard and keep it, and not so that his sight should be darkened by them in such a way that he can no longer see the truth of things. And because shields are commonly of round form, although that of Minerva is sometimes seen made otherwise. Martianus wrote that the shield on Minerva's arm signified that the World, which is likewise of round form, is governed with the utmost and infinite prudence, and not by chance, as Democritus and Epicurus held. And the spear means that the prudent man can do harm to another even from afar; or else that the force of prudence is so great that it penetrates every hardness of the most difficult things, and often rises so high that it reaches to Heaven. Whence Claudian made Minerva's spear so long and high that it passed beyond the clouds. And Homer, perhaps to express this even better, imagines that Minerva, wishing to go to Telemachus, in order to put into his mind that he should go seek Ulysses his father, puts on her feet the golden winged sandals, of that same kind which we have said are shown in the image of Mercury, and carries with her nothing else but the spear. It is found also in Marcus Tullius, where he writes of the nature of the Gods, that there was a certain Minerva (since he tells of five) who was depicted as having wings on her feet. Pausanias likewise writes that there was a long spear in the hand of that image of Minerva, which had upon its helmet, as I have already said, the Sphinx and the Griffins; and he goes on describing it, that it stood upright in a certain tunic that covered it entirely down to the ground, and beneath the breastplate (which lay at its feet) was the shield, and they add also the Owl, and that at the base of the spear was a serpent. From which Demosthenes took his argument, when he was forced to go into exile, saying that Minerva, who was the very deity proper to Athens, delighted overmuch in three strange creatures, which were the Owl, the Serpent, and the People: for in the republic of Athens the people had a great deal to do, and took things in the worst way whenever it felt itself offended. But, as I have already said of the Owl, so I say of the Serpent, that it was given to Minerva as a sign of shrewdness and prudence. Whence in Rome, before the great image of Minerva, down at her feet lay the Serpent, all coiled upon itself, save that it raised its head up behind the shield which she held on her arm, as Servius says, where Virgil has it that the two serpents which killed Laocoon and his sons went straight to the temple of Minerva, and there placed themselves at the feet of the Goddess, and beneath the shield. Concerning the tunic which she wears with the breastplate over it, Herodotus writes that the Greeks took this manner of dress from the women of Africa who dwell around the Tritonis marsh, nor is there any other

difference, save that the tunic beneath these is of skins, and the fringes, or borders, let us say, of the jerkin above are not of little serpents, but of leather cut into narrow strips, which jerkin those women of Africa likewise used to make of goat leather, and therefore the Greeks called it Aegis, for "Aega" among them signifies "Goat," and this is what we have called the breastplate, which perhaps had its borders of small serpents round about, as Herodotus seems to have meant to say, when he set the difference, as I have said, between the dress of the African women and Minerva's attire. To which the ancients further added upon the breast the Gorgon, which was the head of Medusa, hairy with serpents, which thrust forth its tongue, and they also at times placed it upon the shield, which was likewise called Aegis by some; for Diodorus writes that Jove covered it with the skin of the goat Amalthea, and then gave it to Minerva. But more often by Aegis is meant the armor of the breast, which Hyginus writes was so called not from "Aega," taken for "Goat"; but from a daughter of the Sun of this name, who was, as the fables relate, of marvelous whiteness with a stupendous splendor, yet not beautiful however, but rather so horrible to see that as soon as she showed herself to the Titans, enemies of Jove, they all remained terrified and stunned. Whereupon the earth, entreated by them to remove her from before their eyes, hid her in Crete in a certain cave, where she remained until Jove took her from there, when he wished also to have the head of Medusa, because the Oracle had said that without this he could not conquer the Titans, as indeed he conquered them afterward, and after the victory he gave the Aegis, made of the skin of Aega with the head of Medusa, to Minerva, who thereafter always wore it. Virgil, when he has Vulcan go to set the Cyclopes to work to make arms for Aeneas, as Venus had begged of him, and relates the labors that they then had in hand, which were the thunderbolts of Jove, the chariot of Mars, and the armor of Minerva, which is the same as that of Pallas, speaks thus of it.

And of a Serpent's gilded scales
They fashioned with skill the dread
Aegis, with which Pallas in her wrath
Often arms herself, and the woven serpents;
And the Gorgon's head, which even severed
Rolled its eyes with a dark and fierce look,
They fitted to the Goddess's breast.

And therefore by Gorgon is always meant the head of Medusa, which by sight alone killed others, although Athenaeus writes that among the Nomads in Libya there was a certain beast of this name, similar to

Sheep, or as others would have it, to Calves, with breath so pernicious that it alone killed all other beasts that came near it, and by its gaze likewise slew others, and which, at times, shaking its head, raised before it a certain mane, which, hanging down over its forehead, covered its eyes, as was proved by certain soldiers of Marius, when he marched against Jugurtha, who, pursuing this beast, fell dead the instant they were seen by it. And the people of that country then told its nature to Marius himself, and also helped him to kill it, for they knew that, lying in ambush, one could kill it from afar. Its hide was of such marvelous variety of color that, when sent to Rome, there was no one who knew what manner of beast it had been, and as a marvelous thing it was placed in the temple of Hercules. Proclus the Carthaginian wrote, as Pausanias relates, that among the many and diverse beasts that were in the deserts of Africa, there were also wild and bestial men and women, one of whom he himself had seen brought to Rome, and he was inclined to believe that Medusa had been one of those women, who, having gone to the Tritonis marsh, had there done much harm to the inhabitants of the country, until she was slain by Perseus with Minerva's help, because she was the very deity of that place. Diodorus writes that the Gorgons were warlike women in Africa, who were overcome by Perseus, who also slew Medusa their queen, and this could well be history. But the fables say, as is read in Apollodorus, that the Gorgons were three sisters, of whom Medusa alone could die; the other two, named Euryale and Stheno, were immortal, and all had their heads wrapped in scaly serpents, had teeth as large as a boar's, hands of bronze, wings of gold, with which they flew at their pleasure, and turned to stone whoever was seen by them, and that Perseus, having found them asleep, cut off Medusa's head, carried it away, and then gave it to Minerva; by whom he was greatly aided in doing this, for from her he had the shield, just as from Mercury he had the curved sword, and the winged sandals, the helmet of Orcus, which made its wearer invisible, and a certain wallet, in which he carried the terrible head — from certain nymphs, who were taught to him by the three sisters of the Gorgons, in order to get back the eye and the tooth stolen from them by him; for of these it is read that they were born old women, and had but one eye and one tooth between them, and made use of it in turn, now the one, now the other. And for this reason there was, in a certain part of Greece, as Pausanias writes, in the temple of Minerva, a statue of Perseus, to whom, as though he were then about to go into Africa against Medusa, certain Nymphs gave a helmet, and fastened the winged sandals to his feet. They also say — and this is the more common fable — that of three most beautiful sisters, called the Gorgons after certain Islands of like name, where they dwelt, Medusa was the most beautiful,

beautiful, and had hair of gold. Whence Neptune, having fallen in love with her, lay with her in the temple of Minerva, who, thereby greatly scorned and angered, made Medusa, who before had been beautiful and pleasing to behold, become entirely terrible and frightful, changing her golden hair into ugly serpents: and willed that whoever thereafter looked upon her should at once be turned to stone; but the world, unable to bear so strange a monster, had it slain by Perseus with the help I have told, who gave the head to Minerva, who thereafter always bore it upon her shield, or upon the breast of her breastplate. Which, when Homer has this Goddess arm herself to go against the Trojans, he says is surrounded by horrible dread, and that, besides the head of Medusa, there is within it also spirited boldness, and sure courage, and dreadful threats, all things proper to the Goddess of wars, as is Victory too. Whence Pausanias says that the Athenians placed it upon her breast together with the head of Medusa, and that among the Eleans it stood beside her without wings. Which things show the power of knowledge and of prudence: for this, by its marvelous works and wise counsels, makes others marvel, and remain almost motionless as stone with wonder, so that it then easily obtains whatever it wishes, provided it knows how to set it forth fittingly, which this horrible head shows by thrusting forth its tongue. And it was at times covered by the fair mantle which they placed about the Goddess, called by the ancients the Peplos, and this was a kind of garment, used about the images of the Gods, without sleeves, as Lactantius says commenting on Statius, white, and all spotted with gilded bosses, which the matrons made with their own hand, and offered then every third year. But because this was an invention of the Athenians, to whom Minerva was the principal deity, the name Peplos was more often taken for that great garment, or mantle, whichever it was, which was offered and consecrated to this Goddess every five years with the most solemn ceremony, although Suidas says that it was not a garment, but the sail of a certain ship, which at that same time, as I have said, was prepared with the most beautiful adornments in honor of Minerva at certain of her festivals, and the ancients also had the custom of offering the Peplos when, in some grave danger, they wished to obtain the Goddess's favor. Whence Homer has it that Hecuba, by the counsel of Helenus her son, and a seer, when she sees the Trojans being driven by the Greeks even within the walls, prepares from her most beautiful and most precious garments a great and rich Peplos, and, accompanied by all the noblest matrons, carries it to the temple of Pallas, and there has it offered by Theano, wife of Antenor, a woman then held among the Trojan women in the greatest veneration, and all together pray the Goddess that she may be favorable to them. Which thing was imitated by Virgil, when he depicts the war of Troy at Carthage in the temple of Juno, saying;

Meanwhile Juno, with disheveled hair,
The women of Ilium to the temple of unjust
Pallas, and humbly all the Peplos
Carried to the Goddess, ever with their hands
Beating their grieving breasts.

And on this solemn mantle the Athenians were wont to weave, embroider, or paint Enceladus, or whatever other Giant it might be, who was slain by Minerva; besides which at times they also depicted there those who had been most valiant in battle, and thereby deserved greater glory. That giant was a man from the waist up, and a serpent for the rest, for thus all those Giants are described by the poets, who had the boldness to go and assail Heaven. Whence Suidas relates of Commodus, an Emperor insolent and cruel beyond measure, who, to be called Hercules, and son of Jove, often wore the lion's skin, and carried the club in hand, with which he killed many men for his pleasure, and, as though wishing to seem then fighting for the Gods, had their thighs and legs first dressed in the form of an asp or serpent, so that they might represent the Giants. Whom Apollodorus describes as having horrible and fearsome faces, with long hair hanging down to their shoulders, and with thick beards descending over their dreadful breasts. And by their lower half is understood that impious men, despisers of God, never do anything that is straight, nor just, nor honest, but quite the contrary, and therefore resemble the Serpent, which cannot raise itself from the ground, nor walk straight, but must, in going, twist itself entirely. And to these Minerva brings death, because they always remain in the darkness of human ignorance, and never lift their eyes to that divine light which guides others to a glorious and eternal life, and this is the help and favor which Minerva gives to whoever goes to her, as is read of Perseus, of whom I have already spoken, and of Bellerophon, who slew the Chimera, having had from her the horse Pegasus, tamed and fit to ride. Whence those of Corinth, as Pausanias writes, had an image of Minerva all of wood (except the face, hands, and feet, which were of white marble), called by them Bridler, because they said that she was the first to bridle the horse Pegasus, and gave him to Bellerophon. Prometheus likewise, with her help, went up into Heaven, and stole the fire of the Sun's chariot, with which he then gave the arts to the world, which are therefore said to have come from Minerva, because human ingenuity has found all that is done among us, and finds still every day, and makes it, by means of fire, since in all arts two things are needed: one is industry and invention, the other is putting into practice, and doing that which

that ingenuity has devised. That is understood as Minerva, and this as Vulcan, that is, as fire. For under the name of Vulcan is understood fire, which is for us the instrument for making all things, because fire warms and shines, and, light and heat being lacking, nothing can be done. It is indeed true that art cannot always put into effect all that ingenuity discovers, because art is bound to the body, and cannot depart from it, nor do more than it is able, but ingenuity often leaves it behind, and discourses at its pleasure, considering the works of nature, and what God does, and at times imagines that it too can do similar things, of which, however, no effect is ever seen, because these are vain imaginings. Whence it was feigned by the fables that Vulcan could never join with Minerva, although he made every effort to do so, Jove having granted it to him. But the ancients did not therefore cease to place the images of both often in one and the same temple. And Plato likewise sets them together, saying in his Atlanticus that both are equally Deities of Athens; for there at that time all the arts were no less practiced than the study of the sciences flourished. As is also read of Neptune and of Minerva, that by order of Jove both together had the governance of Athens. For which reason the Athenians stamped on their coins the head of Minerva on one side, and on the other the Trident, the emblem of Neptune, whom they also called King, and to Minerva they gave the name of Civic and Urban, inasmuch as it is necessary to govern cities peaceably, and with prudence. Which is no less needful in private houses, and therefore, both on the doors of these, and on those of the City, the ancients were accustomed to paint Minerva, and they painted Mars outside at the Villas, showing in this way that war must always be kept as far off as possible; and because the Romans were careful not to keep in the city those Deities whom they thought to have charge of harmful things, they had outside it the temple of Bellona, and that of Mars too. But of this latter there was also indeed one within the City, where he was worshipped as peaceful, and called Quirinus, as I already wrote in the chapter on Flavius, and gave the reason for the one and for the other. And of him I shall tell how he was depicted, after I shall have spoken of Vulcan, of whom it is read thus in Eusebius. They say Vulcan is the virtue and power of fire, and they make him a statue in the form of a man with a cap on his head of sky-blue color as a sign of the revolution of the heavens, among which is found the true fire, pure and sincere: a thing that cannot be said of this fire which we have, because it does not sustain itself, but continually needs new fuel to nourish and sustain it. And Vulcan was feigned lame, because such the flame appears to be, since, burning, it does not go straight upward, but twists, and thrashes about this way and that, because it is not pure and light, as
fix.after:
Images of Mercury and of Minerva — he the god of Eloquence, she of Prudence, inventress of the good arts; signifying that Eloquence and Prudence must needs be joined together, if words are to be of benefit to human actions.

MINERVA

It is said that among the marvellous things given by God to human Nature, two are greatly to be admired: one is speech, the other the use of the hands. For the one, expressing the mind's conceptions with marvellous force, persuades others of what it wishes; the other, with much industry, puts into effect all that can preserve men's lives, and defend them, as are all the arts already discovered, or that will be discovered in the future. And because fine speech does not benefit, but rather harms, and does evil whenever it is not accompanied by good will and by prudence, nor can prudence be of use to the world when it does not know how to persuade others to flee evil and follow good, and to do those things that are needful to civil life, the ancients showed this by coupling together Mercury, of whom I have already spoken, and Minerva, of whom I shall now speak, held to be the Goddess of prudence, and inventress of all the arts. And therefore, joining together the statues of both these Gods, they made of them one, and called it by a Greek word Hermathena, because the Greeks call Mercury Hermes, and Minerva Athena, and they kept it in the Academies, to show to those who exercised there that eloquence and prudence must be joined together, since the one by itself profits little, and the other by itself likewise often harms, and perhaps always, as Marcus Tullius discourses at some length at the beginning of his work On Invention, who also writes to his Atticus of this statue, as I have said, in this manner: "Your Hermathena pleases me greatly, and is so well placed in the Academy that it seems to hold it entirely." Wishing, then, to make Minerva, either alone, or accompanied by Mercury, she should be made with an almost masculine face, and very severe in aspect, with eyes of sky-blue colour, which Homer always gives her as her own. And Pausanias, after having written of a certain image of Minerva that was in Athens in the temple of Vulcan, adds that he had

found a certain fable, which makes her the daughter of Neptune, and that she had sky-blue eyes, because such were also her Father's. But Cicero, where he speaks of the nature of the Gods, says that Minerva's eyes were grey-green (caesii), and Neptune's blue (caerulei), which might show some difference between them, but I do not believe, however, that it was great, for both words among the Latins signify a light greenish colour, such as is seen in the eyes of cats and owls; unless they wish perhaps to say that in Minerva's eyes there was a more fiery brilliance, similar to that shown by the eyes of Lions. Let her likewise be made armed, with a long spear in hand, and with a crystal shield on her arm, as Ovid does, who has her depict herself in this very way, when she competes in embroidery against Arachne, saying, continuing that design.

She makes herself with spear, and with shield, and arms
Her head with a helmet, and her breast with a breastplate,

Which things show the nature of the prudent man, as I shall say later. Claudian too, and others, have described Minerva in the same manner, perhaps taking, as they have often done with many other things, the likeness from Homer, who, when he has her, persuaded by Juno, go to aid the Greeks against Mars, who then fought for the Trojans, describes her in the form of a valiant warrior, and gives her a helmet on her head all gilded, because the wit of the shrewd man, armed with wise counsels, easily defends himself from whatever might harm him, and shines entirely in the fine and worthy works he does. And the gold upon Minerva's helmet also signifies that she is often taken for the divine splendour which illuminates human intellects, and from which comes all prudence, and all knowledge. It was also imagined that Minerva was born from the head of Jove, as Pausanias writes, stating there was an image of this on the acropolis of Athens; Vulcan having opened it for her with a sharp diamond axe, without the service of a wife, because the intellective power of the soul resides in the brain; and she descends, and all her knowledge, from the supreme intellect, which is Jove: since all wisdom comes from God, and is born from the mouth of the Most High, not from these low and earthly things shown through Juno. And this is a better disposition than that which Martianus made in contempt of women, who, perhaps not being too great a friend of theirs, says, imagining that Minerva was born without a mother, because women have no counsel, nor any prudence; or perhaps he said this so as to follow Aristotle, who writes in his Ethics that women have no good counsel at all. Whom I do not dare to oppose, but I say well that many women in our times show themselves so prudent,

As for her, to return to his design, Apuleius places upon her helm a garland of olive, for this tree was given as her own by the ancients, because she was its discoverer, as Virgil also calls her, and as the fable tells of the contest that was between her and Neptune over the possession of Athens; where Herodotus writes that it was that same olive which Minerva then made spring up, and which burned together with the City already burned by the Persians, but that on that same day it put forth new shoots again, and grew to the height of two cubits. And some say that this was so feigned because Minerva was the first to show the way of pressing oil from olives, and also because the sciences cannot be acquired without frequent study and long vigils. Whence it is read that also in Athens there was dedicated to this Goddess a golden lamp, which burned continually, yet they put in no more oil than once a year, and this was, says Pausanias, because the wick was of a certain kind of flax that is not consumed by fire. And the same author relates that among the Corinthians, when Epopeus, for a certain victory, had made a temple to Minerva, he prayed her to show some sign of holding it dear, and that straightway there before the dedicated temple there sprang forth from the earth a shoot of olive. Whence it may be seen that rightly was the olive given to her, not only for the study of knowledge alone, but also for the practice of the arts discovered by her, such as spinning, sewing, weaving, and doing other things proper to women. For which the Greeks had a great wooden statue of this Goddess seated upon a high seat, holding a distaff with both hands: and the Romans, on a certain day of the feasts celebrated in March to Minerva, had the mistresses feast their maidservants, and serve them with their own hand, as if wishing to show that they acknowledged the benefit they drew from their maidservants through spinning, weaving, sewing, and doing the other things of which she had been the inventress; and that the maidservants likewise should have from her this reward for the labors endured all year in the arts found by her. The Owl too was at times placed upon Minerva's helm, as a bird proper to her and so loved by her that, whether upon her head or at her feet, she almost always has it with her; the reason for which some hold to be that in Athens, a city dear to this Goddess above all others, as the name shows, which she had in common with it, for the study of the sciences and the good arts, which there had already long flourished, there was a great abundance of these birds. Whence arose the proverb of "carrying owls to Athens," said of those who wish to give another that of which he already has great abundance. But the fables say that Minerva first loved the Crow, having made her become a bird from a beautiful maiden, who was

had first been a beautiful maiden, to defend her from the force of Neptune, who, having fallen in love with her, chased after her along the seashore, and kept her in his service until she accused the daughters of Cercops: whereupon the Goddess, angered then at the sorry office performed by this maiden, straightway made her, who had before been white, turn black as she is now, and drove her away from herself, and took the Owl in her place, whence there arose, and still endures, a most grave enmity between these two birds. And the Owl signifies the wisdom and good counsel of the prudent man, as is read in Justin, that an Owl having flown onto the spear of Hiero the first time that, still a youth, he went to war, it was interpreted that he would be of very shrewd counsel; and it proved true, for he became King of Syracuse, although born of low station. And because Minerva's eyes are of the same color as the Owl's, which sees very well by night, it is understood that the wise man sees and knows things however difficult and hidden they may be, and that, having lifted from his mind the veil of lies, he penetrates to Truth with the sight of the intellect; for she remains hidden, and does not let herself be seen by everyone: whence Democritus placed her in the depth of a well, saying that from there she never came out, unless Time, or Saturn her father (as Plutarch says), drew her out of it at times. And Hippocrates, writing to a friend of his, depicts Truth in the form of a woman beautiful, tall, honestly adorned, and all bright and shining, but most of all in the eyes, for these seem two most lucid stars, and he adds then concerning Opinion, that she is likewise a woman, but not so beautiful, nor ugly either, but shows herself all bold and quick to seize upon whatever presents itself to her. In Epiphanius it is read that certain Heretics depicted Truth with Greek letters in this manner. They set it that alpha and omega were the head, and beta and psi the neck, and so, coming down, they formed the whole body, always placing those two letters that, in order, come closest to the first and to the last. And Philostratus, saying that Truth was painted in the sacred cave of Amphiaraus, makes her clothed in the whitest garments, and elsewhere then calls her the mother of Virtue. Who was likewise believed a Goddess by the ancients, and worshipped, and to her, as to the other Gods, the Romans set up a temple before that of Honor, which, having been vowed to both of these by Marcellus, as Valerius Maximus relates, had to be made into two, because the Pontiffs said that religion did not allow a single temple to be dedicated to two Divinities: since, should some prodigy occur in it, one could not know to which of the two the sacrifice ought to be made. So that to Virtue and to Honor was given each its own separate place, and into this latter none could enter save by passing through the former, wishing thereby to show that there is no other way to acquire honor than that of virtue, as that is the

for the prudent man ought not to waste time in many vain words; but, keeping silent, must consider things very well before reasoning about them, and then say of them only what is needful. This perhaps the statue of this Goddess that was among the Messenians meant to show, which, as Pausanias describes it, held a Crow in its hand, as though to say that speech ought to be so held in the hand of the wise man, that he may loosen or restrain it according to whatever occasion presents itself as the need requires. Minerva also had a long spear in her hand, as I said, which all the Poets give her; and Apuleius likewise describes her as brandishing this in her hand, and, raising her arm, lifting her shield, and makes two go with her, like children, who with bare knives in hand seem to go threatening: of whom one is Dread, the other Fear, for wars are never without these. Wherefore Statius, imagining that Mars, commanded by Jove, goes to stir up war between the Argives and the Thebans, says that he took Dread and Terror with him, and made them go before him, and describes him in part, and in part depicts the feelings that come from him, in this manner.

From the cruel rabble that surrounds him he chooses
Terror, and sends him before on horseback,
Whose power none can match,
In making others fear, let alone surpass him.
Through him it seems that man scorns the truth,
If in the timid breast there come to dwell
The horrendous monster, who has voices without number,
And hands ever ready and bold for evil.
Not one alone is always his face,
But many, and all in varied aspects,
Which change at every hour, provided it please him
To match them to his dreadful words;
Which drive so forcefully into human hearts
That they are compelled to give them full belief.
And with such dread he often assails

The Cities, which then believe every evil,
Will believe that there is no longer but a single Sun,
And what is not shall seem to them a vision,
If wretched mortals to the words
Of dread Terror, rarely true,
Lend their ears, and believe that a cloud
Steals away the stars, whereby we must all then fall,
That the earth trembles in fear, and quakes entirely;
And with it the forests too are shaken.

Pausanias states that Terror was made in two ways by the ancients: one with a Lion's head, which was so carved, as he says, among the Eleans on the shield of Agamemnon: the other with the face and dress of a woman, but more frightful than can be told. And such an image of Dread the Corinthians dedicated to the children of Medea, slain by them on account of the pernicious gifts which they bore to the daughter of Creon, whereby she perished together with the whole royal house. But Fear was not always believed to be harmful, for Plutarch writes that it was worshipped by the Lacedaemonians, not because they feared it, as they did certain other Demons, whom they wished kept far from the city, but because they thought that the Republic was preserved by it, when the laws and the Magistrates were held in fear. Whence it was that the Ephors, who were the highest magistracy, upon entering office, at once (as Aristotle says) commanded, and had it proclaimed throughout the city, that everyone should shave his beard and be obedient to the laws; so that they themselves should not be forced to do harm to any person, and they did this to accustom the young to obey even in trifling matters. Besides this, the ancients did not believe that true courage lay in fearing nothing at all, but rather in being afraid to do something unworthy: and they held that he ought to be bolder against enemies who feared to offend the laws, than he who took no account of them at all; and that the fear of acquiring a bad name made men stouter in bearing every toil and every danger. And this is the fear that peoples ought to have; and for this the Lacedaemonians placed the temple of Fear beside the house of the Ephors. And of this perhaps Tullus Hostilius too, King of the Romans, had understanding, when he ordained (as Lactantius relates) that Fear and Pallor should be worshipped together, since it rarely happens that he who is afraid does not turn pale. And well did he deserve, having found them so fine, as Lactantius himself says, to have his Gods always with him, and that they should never abandon him. But returning to Minerva, she shows, while brandishing the spear, and raising the shield with the company that Apuleius gives her, the threats of war; and if we consider it

we consider it in peace, the shield, which was of most lucid crystal, and covered the body from whatever might have come to offend it, showed that the mind of the prudent man is covered by earthly limbs only so as to guard and keep it, and not so that his sight should be darkened by them in such a way that he can no longer see the truth of things. And because shields are commonly of round form, although that of Minerva is sometimes seen made otherwise. Martianus wrote that the shield on Minerva's arm signified that the World, which is likewise of round form, is governed with the utmost and infinite prudence, and not by chance, as Democritus and Epicurus held. And the spear means that the prudent man can do harm to another even from afar; or else that the force of prudence is so great that it penetrates every hardness of the most difficult things, and often rises so high that it reaches to Heaven. Whence Claudian made Minerva's spear so long and high that it passed beyond the clouds. And Homer, perhaps to express this even better, imagines that Minerva, wishing to go to Telemachus, in order to put into his mind that he should go seek Ulysses his father, puts on her feet the golden winged sandals, of that same kind which we have said are shown in the image of Mercury, and carries with her nothing else but the spear. It is found also in Marcus Tullius, where he writes of the nature of the Gods, that there was a certain Minerva (since he tells of five) who was depicted as having wings on her feet. Pausanias likewise writes that there was a long spear in the hand of that image of Minerva, which had upon its helmet, as I have already said, the Sphinx and the Griffins; and he goes on describing it, that it stood upright in a certain tunic that covered it entirely down to the ground, and beneath the breastplate (which lay at its feet) was the shield, and they add also the Owl, and that at the base of the spear was a serpent. From which Demosthenes took his argument, when he was forced to go into exile, saying that Minerva, who was the very deity proper to Athens, delighted overmuch in three strange creatures, which were the Owl, the Serpent, and the People: for in the republic of Athens the people had a great deal to do, and took things in the worst way whenever it felt itself offended. But, as I have already said of the Owl, so I say of the Serpent, that it was given to Minerva as a sign of shrewdness and prudence. Whence in Rome, before the great image of Minerva, down at her feet lay the Serpent, all coiled upon itself, save that it raised its head up behind the shield which she held on her arm, as Servius says, where Virgil has it that the two serpents which killed Laocoon and his sons went straight to the temple of Minerva, and there placed themselves at the feet of the Goddess, and beneath the shield. Concerning the tunic which she wears with the breastplate over it, Herodotus writes that the Greeks took this manner of dress from the women of Africa who dwell around the Tritonis marsh, nor is there any other

difference, save that the tunic beneath these is of skins, and the fringes, or borders, let us say, of the jerkin above are not of little serpents, but of leather cut into narrow strips, which jerkin those women of Africa likewise used to make of goat leather, and therefore the Greeks called it Aegis, for "Aega" among them signifies "Goat," and this is what we have called the breastplate, which perhaps had its borders of small serpents round about, as Herodotus seems to have meant to say, when he set the difference, as I have said, between the dress of the African women and Minerva's attire. To which the ancients further added upon the breast the Gorgon, which was the head of Medusa, hairy with serpents, which thrust forth its tongue, and they also at times placed it upon the shield, which was likewise called Aegis by some; for Diodorus writes that Jove covered it with the skin of the goat Amalthea, and then gave it to Minerva. But more often by Aegis is meant the armor of the breast, which Hyginus writes was so called not from "Aega," taken for "Goat"; but from a daughter of the Sun of this name, who was, as the fables relate, of marvelous whiteness with a stupendous splendor, yet not beautiful however, but rather so horrible to see that as soon as she showed herself to the Titans, enemies of Jove, they all remained terrified and stunned. Whereupon the earth, entreated by them to remove her from before their eyes, hid her in Crete in a certain cave, where she remained until Jove took her from there, when he wished also to have the head of Medusa, because the Oracle had said that without this he could not conquer the Titans, as indeed he conquered them afterward, and after the victory he gave the Aegis, made of the skin of Aega with the head of Medusa, to Minerva, who thereafter always wore it. Virgil, when he has Vulcan go to set the Cyclopes to work to make arms for Aeneas, as Venus had begged of him, and relates the labors that they then had in hand, which were the thunderbolts of Jove, the chariot of Mars, and the armor of Minerva, which is the same as that of Pallas, speaks thus of it.

And of a Serpent's gilded scales
They fashioned with skill the dread
Aegis, with which Pallas in her wrath
Often arms herself, and the woven serpents;
And the Gorgon's head, which even severed
Rolled its eyes with a dark and fierce look,
They fitted to the Goddess's breast.

And therefore by Gorgon is always meant the head of Medusa, which by sight alone killed others, although Athenaeus writes that among the Nomads in Libya there was a certain beast of this name, similar to

Sheep, or as others would have it, to Calves, with breath so pernicious that it alone killed all other beasts that came near it, and by its gaze likewise slew others, and which, at times, shaking its head, raised before it a certain mane, which, hanging down over its forehead, covered its eyes, as was proved by certain soldiers of Marius, when he marched against Jugurtha, who, pursuing this beast, fell dead the instant they were seen by it. And the people of that country then told its nature to Marius himself, and also helped him to kill it, for they knew that, lying in ambush, one could kill it from afar. Its hide was of such marvelous variety of color that, when sent to Rome, there was no one who knew what manner of beast it had been, and as a marvelous thing it was placed in the temple of Hercules. Proclus the Carthaginian wrote, as Pausanias relates, that among the many and diverse beasts that were in the deserts of Africa, there were also wild and bestial men and women, one of whom he himself had seen brought to Rome, and he was inclined to believe that Medusa had been one of those women, who, having gone to the Tritonis marsh, had there done much harm to the inhabitants of the country, until she was slain by Perseus with Minerva's help, because she was the very deity of that place. Diodorus writes that the Gorgons were warlike women in Africa, who were overcome by Perseus, who also slew Medusa their queen, and this could well be history. But the fables say, as is read in Apollodorus, that the Gorgons were three sisters, of whom Medusa alone could die; the other two, named Euryale and Stheno, were immortal, and all had their heads wrapped in scaly serpents, had teeth as large as a boar's, hands of bronze, wings of gold, with which they flew at their pleasure, and turned to stone whoever was seen by them, and that Perseus, having found them asleep, cut off Medusa's head, carried it away, and then gave it to Minerva; by whom he was greatly aided in doing this, for from her he had the shield, just as from Mercury he had the curved sword, and the winged sandals, the helmet of Orcus, which made its wearer invisible, and a certain wallet, in which he carried the terrible head — from certain nymphs, who were taught to him by the three sisters of the Gorgons, in order to get back the eye and the tooth stolen from them by him; for of these it is read that they were born old women, and had but one eye and one tooth between them, and made use of it in turn, now the one, now the other. And for this reason there was, in a certain part of Greece, as Pausanias writes, in the temple of Minerva, a statue of Perseus, to whom, as though he were then about to go into Africa against Medusa, certain Nymphs gave a helmet, and fastened the winged sandals to his feet. They also say — and this is the more common fable — that of three most beautiful sisters, called the Gorgons after certain Islands of like name, where they dwelt, Medusa was the most beautiful,

beautiful, and had hair of gold. Whence Neptune, having fallen in love with her, lay with her in the temple of Minerva, who, thereby greatly scorned and angered, made Medusa, who before had been beautiful and pleasing to behold, become entirely terrible and frightful, changing her golden hair into ugly serpents: and willed that whoever thereafter looked upon her should at once be turned to stone; but the world, unable to bear so strange a monster, had it slain by Perseus with the help I have told, who gave the head to Minerva, who thereafter always bore it upon her shield, or upon the breast of her breastplate. Which, when Homer has this Goddess arm herself to go against the Trojans, he says is surrounded by horrible dread, and that, besides the head of Medusa, there is within it also spirited boldness, and sure courage, and dreadful threats, all things proper to the Goddess of wars, as is Victory too. Whence Pausanias says that the Athenians placed it upon her breast together with the head of Medusa, and that among the Eleans it stood beside her without wings. Which things show the power of knowledge and of prudence: for this, by its marvelous works and wise counsels, makes others marvel, and remain almost motionless as stone with wonder, so that it then easily obtains whatever it wishes, provided it knows how to set it forth fittingly, which this horrible head shows by thrusting forth its tongue. And it was at times covered by the fair mantle which they placed about the Goddess, called by the ancients the Peplos, and this was a kind of garment, used about the images of the Gods, without sleeves, as Lactantius says commenting on Statius, white, and all spotted with gilded bosses, which the matrons made with their own hand, and offered then every third year. But because this was an invention of the Athenians, to whom Minerva was the principal deity, the name Peplos was more often taken for that great garment, or mantle, whichever it was, which was offered and consecrated to this Goddess every five years with the most solemn ceremony, although Suidas says that it was not a garment, but the sail of a certain ship, which at that same time, as I have said, was prepared with the most beautiful adornments in honor of Minerva at certain of her festivals, and the ancients also had the custom of offering the Peplos when, in some grave danger, they wished to obtain the Goddess's favor. Whence Homer has it that Hecuba, by the counsel of Helenus her son, and a seer, when she sees the Trojans being driven by the Greeks even within the walls, prepares from her most beautiful and most precious garments a great and rich Peplos, and, accompanied by all the noblest matrons, carries it to the temple of Pallas, and there has it offered by Theano, wife of Antenor, a woman then held among the Trojan women in the greatest veneration, and all together pray the Goddess that she may be favorable to them. Which thing was imitated by Virgil, when he depicts the war of Troy at Carthage in the temple of Juno, saying;

Meanwhile, with disheveled hair, there went
The women of Ilium to the temple of unjust
Pallas, and humbly all the Peplos
Carried to the Goddess, ever with their hands
Beating their grieving breasts.

And on this solemn mantle the Athenians were wont to weave, embroider, or paint Enceladus, or whatever other Giant it might be, who was slain by Minerva; besides which at times they also depicted there those who had been most valiant in battle, and thereby deserved greater glory. That giant was a man from the waist up, and a serpent for the rest, for thus all those Giants are described by the poets, who had the boldness to go and assail Heaven. Whence Suidas relates of Commodus, an Emperor insolent and cruel beyond measure, who, to be called Hercules, and son of Jove, often wore the lion's skin, and carried the club in hand, with which he killed many men for his pleasure, and, as though wishing to seem then fighting for the Gods, had their thighs and legs first dressed in the form of an asp or serpent, so that they might represent the Giants. Whom Apollodorus describes as having horrible and fearsome faces, with long hair hanging down to their shoulders, and with thick beards descending over their dreadful breasts. And by their lower half is understood that impious men, despisers of God, never do anything that is straight, nor just, nor honest, but quite the contrary, and therefore resemble the Serpent, which cannot raise itself from the ground, nor walk straight, but must, in going, twist itself entirely. And to these Minerva brings death, because they always remain in the darkness of human ignorance, and never lift their eyes to that divine light which guides others to a glorious and eternal life, and this is the help and favor which Minerva gives to whoever goes to her, as is read of Perseus, of whom I have already spoken, and of Bellerophon, who slew the Chimera, having had from her the horse Pegasus, tamed and fit to ride. Whence those of Corinth, as Pausanias writes, had an image of Minerva all of wood (except the face, hands, and feet, which were of white marble), called by them Bridler, because they said that she was the first to bridle the horse Pegasus, and gave him to Bellerophon. Prometheus likewise, with her help, went up into Heaven, and stole the fire of the Sun's chariot, with which he then gave the arts to the world, which are therefore said to have come from Minerva, because human ingenuity has found all that is done among us, and finds still every day, and makes it, by means of fire, since in all arts two things are needed: one is industry and invention, the other is putting into practice, and doing that which

that ingenuity has devised. That is understood as Minerva, and this as Vulcan, that is, as fire. For under the name of Vulcan is understood fire, which is for us the instrument for making all things, because fire warms and shines, and, light and heat being lacking, nothing can be done. It is indeed true that art cannot always put into effect all that ingenuity discovers, because art is bound to the body, and cannot depart from it, nor do more than it is able, but ingenuity often leaves it behind, and discourses at its pleasure, considering the works of nature, and what God does, and at times imagines that it too can do similar things, of which, however, no effect is ever seen, because these are vain imaginings. Whence it was feigned by the fables that Vulcan could never join with Minerva, although he made every effort to do so, Jove having granted it to him. But the ancients did not therefore cease to place the images of both often in one and the same temple. And Plato likewise sets them together, saying in his Atlanticus that both are equally Deities of Athens; for there at that time all the arts were no less practiced than the study of the sciences flourished. As is also read of Neptune and of Minerva, that by order of Jove both together had the governance of Athens. For which reason the Athenians stamped on their coins the head of Minerva on one side, and on the other the Trident, the emblem of Neptune, whom they also called King, and to Minerva they gave the name of Civic and Urban, inasmuch as it is necessary to govern cities peaceably, and with prudence. Which is no less needful in private houses, and therefore, both on the doors of these, and on those of the City, the ancients were accustomed to paint Minerva, and they painted Mars outside at the Villas, showing in this way that war must always be kept as far off as possible; and because the Romans were careful not to keep in the city those Deities whom they thought to have charge of harmful things, they had outside it the temple of Bellona, and that of Mars too. But of this latter there was also indeed one within the City, where he was worshipped as peaceful, and called Quirinus, as I already wrote in the chapter on Flavius, and gave the reason for the one and for the other. And of him I shall tell how he was depicted, after I shall have spoken of Vulcan, of whom it is read thus in Eusebius. They say Vulcan is the virtue and power of fire, and they make him a statue in the form of a man with a cap on his head of sky-blue color as a sign of the revolution of the heavens, among which is found the true fire, pure and sincere: a thing that cannot be said of this fire which we have, because it does not sustain itself, but continually needs new fuel to nourish and sustain it. And Vulcan was feigned lame, because such the flame appears to be, since, burning, it does not go straight upward, but twists, and thrashes about this way and that, because it is not pure and light, as
